overview:
Headquarters Bottom Position represents a defensive half guard configuration where the bottom practitioner finds themselves trapped in their opponent's 'headquarters' pressure position. This occurs when the top player has established strong knee shield control with their shin across the bottom player's torso while maintaining significant forward pressure. The bottom player is typically on their side or back, using defensive frames to create space and prevent the pass while looking for opportunities to recover full guard or initiate sweeps.

This position is characterized by the bottom player being compressed under the top player's weight distribution through the knee shield, requiring strong defensive framing and hip mobility to maintain guard retention. The bottom practitioner must manage the constant threat of the knee slice pass while simultaneously working to improve their position through re-guarding sequences or sweep attempts. Success in this position demands excellent frame management, timing, and the ability to exploit windows of opportunity when the top player commits to passing pressure.

Headquarters Bottom is considered a transitional defensive position rather than a stable attacking platform. The primary objective is survival and position improvement through systematic defensive protocols, with secondary goals of sweep opportunities when the top player overcommits. Understanding the positional hierarchy and having clear pathways to better positions is essential for effective defense from this challenging bottom position.
state_invariants: Bottom player positioned on their side or back with top player's shin/knee across their torso creating compression and control, limiting mobility and offensive options while requiring constant defensive awareness

Bottom player's far side (non-trapped) leg often used as defensive frame or hook to maintain distance and prevent flattening, while near side leg is controlled or pressured by opponent's knee shield position

Top player maintains forward pressure through knee shield with weight distributed across bottom player's chest/abdomen, creating sustained compression that must be managed through frames and hip movement

Bottom player's arms actively framing against top player's shoulder, hip, or knee to create space and prevent further compression while maintaining enough structure to attempt recovery sequences or sweep entries
prerequisites: Top player has established knee shield position across bottom player's torso from half guard
Bottom player unable to maintain full half guard lockdown or butterfly hooks
Top player applying forward pressure through knee shield creating compression
Bottom player's half guard retention compromised but not fully passed
Frames and defensive posture required to prevent immediate pass completion
key_principles: Maintain active frames on top player's shoulder, hip, or knee to prevent complete flattening and create breathing room for defensive movements
Keep hips mobile and ready to shrimp or bridge to create angles for re-guarding or sweep attempts when opportunities arise
Prevent top player from consolidating weight directly over centerline by maintaining angle and using frames to redirect pressure
Protect underhook position on trapped side when possible to maintain connection and prevent complete isolation
Use far leg (non-trapped side) as active defensive tool through frames, hooks, or shield positions to manage distance and create recovery opportunities
Time defensive movements with top player's weight shifts and pressure adjustments to maximize efficiency and create windows for position improvement
Maintain strong mental focus on position improvement pathways rather than accepting prolonged defensive stalemate

Top player commits fully to knee slice creating underhook opportunity
Top player pulls back to reset pressure allowing hip escape

decision_tree.condition: If top player drives forward with heavy knee slice pressure
If top player maintains static pressure without advancing

common_errors.error: Accepting flat position on back without maintaining active frames
common_errors.consequence: Top player consolidates full pressure making re-guarding nearly impossible and pass completion highly probable
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant frame pressure on top player's shoulder or hip while staying on side to preserve mobility and defensive options

common_errors.error: Using only upper body frames without hip movement
common_errors.consequence: Frames collapse under sustained pressure leading to exhaustion and inevitable pass as static defense fails
common_errors.correction: Coordinate frames with hip shrimping and angle creation to use frames as launching points for movement rather than pure blocking

common_errors.error: Attempting sweeps without establishing proper grips or frames first
common_errors.consequence: Sweep attempts fail immediately while giving up defensive structure allowing top player to advance position easily
common_errors.correction: Build defensive frames and grips systematically before initiating offensive movements ensuring stable platform for attempts

common_errors.error: Allowing top player to control both legs simultaneously
common_errors.consequence: Complete loss of guard structure making any recovery impossible and pass completion immediate
common_errors.correction: Keep far leg active as defensive frame or shield maintaining at least one leg free for defensive movements and position recovery

common_errors.error: Fighting with pure strength against superior pressure position
common_errors.consequence: Rapid energy depletion leading to flattening and easy pass as muscular fatigue undermines defensive capacity
common_errors.correction: Use timing and angles to redirect pressure rather than opposing it directly, conserving energy for critical defensive movements

common_errors.error: Focusing solely on preventing pass without seeking position improvement
common_errors.consequence: Stalemate that favors top player's scoring position and allows them to methodically break down defenses over time
common_errors.correction: Balance defensive priorities with active pursuit of re-guard or sweep opportunities creating dynamic rather than static defense

expert_insights.danaher: Headquarters bottom position represents a critical junction in the half guard passing sequence where defensive priorities must be precisely calibrated. The fundamental error practitioners make is treating this as a stable position worthy of extended occupation rather than recognizing it as a transitional crisis requiring immediate systematic response. Your defensive structure must be built on the principle of creating angles rather than opposing pressure directly - when the top player drives their knee across your torso, your frames are not designed to stop this pressure but rather to redirect it while your hips create the angle necessary for re-guarding sequences. The hierarchy of defensive actions must be clear: first establish frames that prevent complete flattening, second create the angle through hip escape that opens recovery pathways, third exploit the window created by these movements to recover guard structure or enter deep half positions. The most sophisticated defense recognizes that the top player's pressure itself creates opportunities - as they commit weight forward to complete the pass, they necessarily create space behind them that allows deep half entries. Your mental model should categorize every moment in headquarters bottom as either building defensive structure or exploiting offensive windows, never accepting passive survival.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: From competition experience, headquarters bottom is where matches get decided - it's the last stand before your guard gets passed and you're defending side control for the rest of the round. The key is understanding that you're playing on a timer here, and that timer is how long your frames can hold up under sustained pressure. I focus on two main pathways: if they're pressuring hard for the knee slice, I'm going under to deep half because their forward commitment is what gives me that entry. If they're being patient and controlling, I'm working my re-guard with the understanding that I need to create a reaction first - usually by threatening the underhook sweep to get them to post, which opens the path to recover full guard. The biggest mistake I see is guys trying to sweep from here without establishing the proper controls first. You're in a defensive position, so your sweeps need to come from defensive reactions, not offensive initiatives. When I'm drilling this position, I'm focused on making my frames efficient enough that I can maintain them while my hips are working, because the moment your frames collapse is the moment you're defending side control. Competition-wise, if you're in headquarters bottom, you better be working toward something better within 10-15 seconds or you're getting passed by any decent opponent.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Headquarters bottom is actually one of my favorite teaching positions because it forces people to understand the 10th Planet philosophy of never accepting bad positions - you're always working toward something better. From here, I'm immediately thinking about the lockdown if I can get it, or I'm going to electric chair entries if they're putting heavy pressure. The thing about headquarters is it's created by their knee shield, so if you can control that knee or get under it, you've got options. I teach a lot of invisible collar work from here too - if they're pressuring hard, their posture is often compromised and you can threaten the guillotine or darce, which creates the reaction that lets you recover. The deep half entry is huge from here, especially the Jeff Glover style where you're swimming the underhook and going belly down. But the real innovation in this position is recognizing that their pressure can be used against them - when they're driving that knee slice, they're committed and off-balance, which is when the old school sweep becomes available. I also like the rubber guard recovery from here if you can get your leg up and into mission control, because their forward pressure actually helps you lock it in. The key is staying creative and not letting them settle into a rhythm with their passing pressure.

overview: The Headquarters Position (HQ) is a fundamental guard passing control position where the top player controls one of the bottom player's legs while establishing strong base and posture. This position serves as a central hub for multiple passing strategies, creating a systematic approach to bypassing various guard configurations. Headquarters offers exceptional control with relatively low risk, acting as a decision point from which the passer can select the optimal passing route based on the opponent's reactions. The position creates a strategic advantage by limiting the bottom player's defensive options while maintaining multiple offensive pathways. From Headquarters, the passer can flow seamlessly between knee slice, long step, smash pass, and leg weave variations, making it one of the most versatile positions in modern guard passing systems.
state_invariants: One of opponent's legs is controlled and pinned between the top player's legs, with the knee driven toward the mat to restrict hip mobility and prevent guard recovery
The supporting leg is firmly posted wide and away from the opponent's body, creating a stable triangular base that resists off-balancing attempts and sweep mechanics
Upright posture is maintained with spine alignment perpendicular to the mat, weight distributed through the hips rather than hands, preventing forward rolls and maintaining balance
Control hand grips the opponent's knee, thigh, or pants at the knee line, while the opposite hand controls the lapel, collar, or establishes an underhook to prevent frames
Opponent's hips are flattened to the mat or controlled in a way that prevents them from turning into the passer or creating angular escapes through hip movement
prerequisites: Solid understanding of base mechanics and weight distribution principles
Ability to establish and maintain knee-line control against resistance
Familiarity with fundamental guard passing concepts and timing
Recognition of opponent's defensive patterns and guard retention strategies
Competence in grip fighting and hand positioning to establish initial control
key_principles: Control opponent's leg by driving knee toward mat, eliminating their ability to create frames or recover guard structure
Establish strong posting base with opposite leg positioned wide and perpendicular to opponent's body line
Maintain upright posture with strong spine alignment, preventing forward weight shift that creates rolling opportunities
Create and manipulate passing angles by adjusting hip position and weight distribution
Control opponent's hip mobility through strategic placement of trapped leg and pressure application
Neutralize opponent's frames and hooks by maintaining distance with posting hand while controlling with gripping hand
Systematically eliminate defensive options by reading reactions and selecting appropriate passing variations

If opponent remains passive without clear defensive commitment

common_errors.error: Poor knee control with insufficient pressure on opponent's knee line
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to recover guard structure, create frames, or enter into half guard positions that neutralize passing momentum
common_errors.correction: Drive knee firmly toward mat using weight from hips, pinning opponent's knee and restricting hip mobility. Maintain constant downward pressure throughout the passing sequence.

common_errors.error: Excessive forward lean with weight shifted over hands rather than hips
common_errors.consequence: Creates vulnerability to forward rolls, off-balancing sweeps, and granby roll escapes. Compromises base stability and reaction time.
common_errors.correction: Keep spine upright and perpendicular to mat, distributing weight through hips and posting leg. Use hands for balance and control, not weight support.

common_errors.error: Insufficient base width with posting leg too close to opponent's body
common_errors.consequence: Reduces stability against lateral sweeps and makes passer vulnerable to being pushed or pulled off balance during opponent's escape attempts
common_errors.correction: Post supporting leg wide and away from opponent's centerline, creating triangular base. Angle posting foot perpendicular to opponent's body for maximum stability.

common_errors.error: Passive positioning without active pressure or advancing intention
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent time to develop escape sequences, recover guard structures, or create effective defensive frames that prevent progression
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant forward pressure while reading opponent's reactions. Continuously threaten multiple passing options to prevent opponent from settling into defensive patterns.

common_errors.error: Telegraphing pass direction through premature weight shifts or grip changes
common_errors.consequence: Opponent anticipates passing direction and establishes defensive structures or escape routes before passer can complete the technique
common_errors.correction: Maintain neutral position until opponent commits to a defensive pattern, then explosively execute the appropriate counter-pass. Use feints and subtle weight adjustments to disguise intentions.

common_errors.error: Losing connection with trapped leg during transitional moments
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recovers full guard or creates scramble situations that eliminate passing advantages and reset position to neutral
common_errors.correction: Maintain leg control throughout entire passing sequence using consistent pressure. If transitioning grips, ensure new control is established before releasing original grip.

common_errors.error: Inadequate head control or upper body management
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to establish effective frames, create distance, or use collar grips to off-balance and disrupt passing attempts
common_errors.correction: Control opponent's upper body using collar grips, underhooks, or crossface pressure. Prevent opponent from establishing frames by managing distance and controlling head positioning.

expert_insights.danaher: Headquarters represents the central hub of a systematic passing approach, where controlling the opponent's knee-line creates the fundamental decision point in guard passing. The position's power lies not in forcing a specific pass, but in creating a control structure that limits the opponent's defensive options while maintaining multiple offensive pathways. By establishing headquarters, you compress the infinite complexity of guard passing into a finite series of if-then sequences. When opponent extends the leg, execute long step. When they turn toward you, execute knee slice. When they create frames, execute smash pass. This systematic reduction transforms guard passing from a chaotic scramble into a controlled technical progression. The critical principle is maintaining connection with the trapped leg throughout all transitions - this connection is the thread that ties together your entire passing system. Without it, you return to chaos. With it, you have a roadmap through every defensive response.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, headquarters is my favorite position because it puts maximum pressure on my opponent to make decisions while I stay relatively safe and can choose my passing route based on their mistakes. I don't commit heavy pressure initially - I want to float just enough to make them think they can escape, which causes them to show me their defensive strategy. Once they commit to pushing my knee, turning into me, or trying to frame, I already know exactly which pass is going to work. The key is not telegraphing your intention. If they can't tell whether you're going knee slice, long step, or smash pass, they can't defend all three simultaneously. I'll often feint one direction to get them overcommitted, then immediately switch to the now-open passing lane. Against high-level opponents, headquarters also gives me time to control their grips and establish my preferred grip configurations before committing to the pass, which dramatically increases my success rate in the actual passing sequence.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: From headquarters-type positions, I'm always looking for opportunities to create unconventional control angles that traditional passers ignore. While everyone is focused on the standard knee slice or long step, I'm thinking about how to use that trapped leg as an anchor point to create rotational pressure that leads into twister side control or truck position entries. If the opponent is defending the standard passes, they're not ready for you to suddenly change levels and attack their back or go for unconventional leg positions. The 10th Planet approach is to use headquarters as a launching point for creative transitions rather than just a passing position. For example, if they defend the knee slice by turning toward me, instead of forcing the pass I might transition to calf slicer control or even look for the truck entry if they give me their back. Don't get stuck thinking headquarters only leads to side control - it can lead to much more interesting positions if you're willing to think outside the box.

overview:
The Headquarters Position Top (HQ) is a fundamental and highly systematic guard passing control position where the top player controls one of the bottom player's legs while establishing strong base, upright posture, and optimal positioning for multiple passing strategies. Popularized and refined by John Danaher and his students, headquarters serves as the central hub of modern guard passing systems, creating a decision point from which the passer can select the optimal passing route based on the opponent's defensive reactions. The position offers exceptional control with minimal energy expenditure and low risk, functioning as a stable platform for methodical, systematic guard passing rather than explosive or risky passing attempts.

The headquarters position represents a fundamental shift in guard passing philosophy, moving away from commitment-heavy passing attempts toward a more measured, reactive approach that maintains safety while threatening multiple directions simultaneously. From this position, the passer can attack with knee slice passes, leg drag passes, long step passes, or transitions to other passing positions while maintaining the ability to return to headquarters if any single passing attempt is defended. This creates a grinding, systematic pressure that exhausts the bottom player's defensive options over time while keeping the passer safe from sweeps and submissions. The position is equally effective in gi and no-gi contexts, though specific gripping strategies differ between the two formats.
state_invariants: One opponent leg controlled between your legs with their knee pinned to the mat by your shin or knee while your leg wraps around or controls their thigh, eliminating their ability to create angles or recover guard structures

Supporting leg firmly posted wide on the mat in a strong triangular base position, typically at 45-90 degree angle from the controlled leg, providing stability against sweeps and allowing weight distribution that prevents opponent from elevating your hips

Upright posture maintained with spine aligned vertically, head up, and shoulders over hips rather than leaning forward onto opponent, creating structural integrity that prevents opponent from breaking you down or creating sweep angles

Hands actively controlling opponent's upper body through collar grips, sleeve grips, or strategic posts on hips and shoulders, maintaining distance management and preventing opponent from establishing defensive frames or closing distance to initiate guard recovery

Opponent's hips flattened to mat or controlled through combination of leg pressure and upper body control, limiting their mobility and ability to create the hip movement necessary for guard retention or sweep attempts
prerequisites: Solid understanding of base and posture fundamentals in top positions
Familiarity with guard passing mechanics and principles of systematic passing
Recognition of opponent's defensive patterns and common guard retention frames
Knowledge of systematic passing approaches and ability to chain multiple passing attempts
Understanding of leg control mechanics and ability to pin opponent's knee effectively
key_principles: Pin opponent's knee firmly to mat with sustained pressure from shin or knee, eliminating space and preventing hip mobility
Maintain upright posture with aligned spine and head position over hips, never collapsing forward onto opponent
Establish wide, stable base with posted leg creating triangular structure that resists sweeps and provides platform for movement
Control opponent's hip mobility through combination of leg pressure and strategic upper body grips
Systematically eliminate defensive options by threatening multiple passing directions simultaneously
Maintain headquarters as decision hub, returning to position between passing attempts rather than overcommitting to single direction
Use opponent's defensive reactions to inform passing selection, attacking the direction they leave vulnerable

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent extends frames to create distance from upper body
Opponent commits knee shield or attempts to recover full guard
Opponent turtles or turns away to defend initial passing attempt
Opponent attempts to insert second leg back into guard or create butterfly hooks

decision_tree.condition: If opponent extends frames and pushes upper body away creating distance
If opponent commits knee shield or attempts to recover guard structure
If opponent turns away or turtles to defend passing attempt
If opponent attempts to create underhooks or battle for inside position

common_errors.error: Poor knee control with insufficient pressure on opponent's pinned leg
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to recover guard easily as insufficient pressure on their knee permits hip mobility and frame recovery, enabling them to re-establish defensive structures and escape passing sequences
common_errors.correction: Pin their knee firmly to the mat with your shin or knee, maintaining constant downward pressure that eliminates their ability to create angles, move hips, or re-establish guard structures

common_errors.error: Weak base positioning with narrow stance or posted leg too close to body
common_errors.consequence: Creates vulnerability to sweeps and reversals as narrow or imbalanced base makes you unstable during transitions, allowing opponent to elevate hips or create off-balancing angles
common_errors.correction: Post supporting leg wide at 45-90 degree angle creating strong triangular base that distributes weight effectively and provides stable platform resistant to opponent's sweep attempts

common_errors.error: Collapsing forward with poor posture, leaning chest and shoulders onto opponent
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to break down your structure, create frames under your chest, and generate sweep opportunities by controlling your upper body weight and creating leverage angles
common_errors.correction: Maintain upright posture with spine vertical, head up, and shoulders positioned over hips, using structural alignment rather than muscular tension to maintain position

common_errors.error: Overcommitting to single passing direction without maintaining headquarters option
common_errors.consequence: Once committed to failed passing attempt, difficult to recover position and opponent can use your momentum to create sweep opportunities or recover guard completely
common_errors.correction: Maintain ability to return to headquarters between passing attempts, treating each pass as probe rather than all-or-nothing commitment, allowing you to chain multiple attempts systematically

common_errors.error: Poor upper body control allowing opponent to establish strong frames or grips
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can create distance, prevent passing pressure, and initiate guard recovery sequences by controlling your posture and movement through frames and grip advantages
common_errors.correction: Actively control opponent's upper body through strategic collar, sleeve, or posting grips that prevent frame establishment and maintain distance management necessary for effective passing

common_errors.error: Static headquarters position without threatening multiple passing directions
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can focus defensive efforts on single direction, making guard retention easier and reducing effectiveness of passing system
common_errors.correction: Constantly threaten multiple passing directions through subtle weight shifts and positioning adjustments, forcing opponent to make defensive choices that create openings in other directions

expert_insights.danaher: The headquarters position represents a fundamental evolution in guard passing theory, moving away from the traditional commitment-heavy passing attempts toward a more systematic, decision-tree based approach that maintains safety while creating multiple attacking vectors simultaneously. The biomechanical efficiency of headquarters lies in its triangulated base structure combined with the mechanical advantage created by pinning the opponent's knee to the mat, which eliminates their primary tool for creating angles and recovering guard structures. From a systematic standpoint, headquarters serves as what I call a 'passing hub' - a central position from which multiple passes can be initiated with minimal positional risk, allowing the passer to probe defenses methodically and select the optimal passing route based on the opponent's reactions rather than committing blindly to a single direction. The key technical elements are the vertical spinal alignment which prevents breakdown, the wide base which resists sweeps, and the active knee pin which eliminates the bottom player's mobility - together these create a position that can be maintained with minimal energy expenditure while constantly threatening progression.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: I use headquarters as my primary passing position in both gi and no-gi because it allows me to stay safe while threatening multiple passes simultaneously. The opponent never knows which direction I'm passing until I commit, which keeps them reactive and defensive rather than able to launch their own attacks. I emphasize a floating approach to headquarters where I maintain lower pressure initially to bait defensive movements, then commit heavily to specific passes when they overcommit to one direction. The key is being patient in headquarters and not rushing passes before the position is properly established - I'll often spend 30-60 seconds just maintaining headquarters and making small adjustments, forcing my opponent to make the first mistake. When they push my upper body, I slice the knee; when they frame the knee slice, I go long step; when they turtle, I smash pass. This reactive passing from a stable hub is what allowed me to maintain such high passing percentages in ADCC and other elite competitions where guard players are extremely difficult to pass through commitment-based approaches.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: While headquarters is more of a traditional systematic approach compared to the 10th Planet style, I recognize its effectiveness for methodical passing, especially in no-gi contexts where leg entanglement positions are prevalent. I teach students to use headquarters as a transition position but emphasize maintaining constant pressure and movement rather than static control - we're always hunting for the calf slice, the truck position, or transitioning to leg attacks if the opponent over-focuses on defending the pass. The combination of headquarters with quick transitions to leg drags and back steps can create explosive passing sequences that catch opponents off guard, especially when they're expecting the slow, grinding headquarters game. The key innovation I bring to headquarters is not getting too attached to the position and being willing to flow between headquarters and other passing positions dynamically, using it as one tool in a larger passing system rather than the single central hub. We also look for the electric chair and banana split from headquarters when the opponent tries to recover half guard, adding submission threats that traditional headquarters players might miss.

overview: Headquarters Top Position is a strategic guard passing position where the top player establishes dominant control over the bottom player's legs while maintaining safe distance from submissions. This position represents the optimal staging area for initiating passes against half guard and other retention-based guards, providing maximum control with minimal risk. The top player uses their weight distribution, shoulder pressure, and leg control to systematically break down the guard player's defensive structure. Headquarters is characterized by the top player's ability to control both of the bottom player's legs while maintaining posture and balance, creating a stable platform from which to execute a variety of passing attacks. This position has become increasingly important in modern BJJ, particularly in no-gi grappling where it serves as a critical transitional state between standing and fully passed positions.
state_invariants: Top player's hips positioned above and outside the bottom player's legs with weight distributed through the chest and shoulder into opponent's upper body, creating constant downward pressure that limits mobility
Top player's hands controlling both of the bottom player's legs, typically one hand on the knee and one controlling the ankle or shin, establishing bilateral leg control that prevents guard retention

Bottom player's back on the mat with shoulders pinned or heavily weighted, unable to create significant angles or generate offensive attacks due to the top player's shoulder pressure and superior position

Top player maintains upright posture with head above the bottom player's center line, allowing visual control of all escape attempts while keeping safe distance from triangle attacks and other guard submissions
Top player's knees positioned wide and stable on the mat outside the bottom player's hips, creating a low base that resists sweeps while allowing dynamic weight transfer for passing attacks
prerequisites: Successful disengagement from close-range guard (closed guard, half guard, or butterfly guard)
Establishment of distance management to prevent re-engagement of guard
Control of at least one of opponent's legs (typically via grip on knee or ankle)
Posture established with chest over opponent's center line
Opponent's shoulders pinned or heavily pressured to mat
Safe positioning away from triangle and submission threats
key_principles: Maintain constant shoulder pressure into opponent's chest/shoulders to limit mobility and prevent re-guard
Control both of opponent's legs simultaneously to eliminate guard retention options
Keep hips mobile and ready to transition in any direction based on opponent's defensive reactions
Distribute weight through chest and shoulders rather than hands to maintain heavy pressure while keeping hands free for grips
Maintain safe distance from opponent's hips to avoid triangle attacks while staying close enough to pressure effectively
Use wide knee base for stability while remaining ready to drive forward or circle for passing angles
Monitor opponent's hands constantly to prevent them from establishing frames or creating space

common_errors.error: Placing too much weight on hands instead of chest and shoulders
common_errors.consequence: Reduces effective pressure on opponent, allows them to create frames and recover guard easily, and tires out arms unnecessarily
common_errors.correction: Drive weight through chest and shoulder into opponent's upper body, keeping hands light for grips and control while using body weight for pressure

common_errors.error: Positioning hips too close to opponent's hips
common_errors.consequence: Exposes passer to triangle attacks, makes it easier for opponent to recover guard or create scrambles
common_errors.correction: Keep hips elevated and positioned away from opponent's hips, maintaining safe distance while still applying shoulder pressure

common_errors.error: Failing to control both of opponent's legs simultaneously
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to easily recover guard by inserting free leg for knee shield or butterfly hook
common_errors.correction: Establish bilateral leg control with both hands on opponent's knees, ankles, or shins before attempting to pass

common_errors.error: Rushing the pass without establishing proper control first
common_errors.consequence: Leads to scrambles, re-guards, or worse positions as opponent capitalizes on improper weight distribution
common_errors.correction: Take time to establish heavy shoulder pressure and solid leg control before initiating passing movement

common_errors.error: Keeping knees too close together, creating narrow base
common_errors.consequence: Makes position unstable and susceptible to sweeps or opponent's attempts to create angles
common_errors.correction: Maintain wide knee base outside opponent's hips for maximum stability and balance

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to establish strong grips on passing leg or arm
common_errors.consequence: Gives opponent leverage to prevent passes and potentially sweep or submit
common_errors.correction: Constantly monitor and break opponent's grips while preventing them from establishing strong control points

common_errors.error: Committing too early to one passing direction
common_errors.consequence: Telegraphs intention and allows opponent to defend effectively in anticipated direction
common_errors.correction: Maintain multi-directional threat by keeping hips mobile and being ready to change passing angle based on opponent's reactions

training_drills.name: Headquarters Establishment Drill
training_drills.description: Partner starts in half guard. Top player works to establish headquarters position by creating distance, controlling legs, and applying shoulder pressure. Bottom player provides progressive resistance. Reset and repeat.

training_drills.name: Multi-Directional Passing from Headquarters
training_drills.description: From established headquarters, top player practices transitioning between different passing attacks (knee slice, long step, smash, leg weave) based on coach's calls or bottom player's defensive reactions. Focus on maintaining control throughout transitions.

training_drills.name: Headquarters Retention Against Re-Guards
training_drills.description: Bottom player actively attempts to recover guard using various methods (knee shield recovery, deep half entry, reverse de la riva). Top player must maintain headquarters position and prevent re-guard through proper pressure and leg control.

training_drills.name: Pressure Application Drill
training_drills.description: From headquarters, top player focuses solely on applying maximum shoulder pressure while maintaining proper positioning. Bottom player provides feedback on pressure effectiveness. Emphasis on weight distribution through chest rather than hands.

expert_insights.danaher: Headquarters position represents the culmination of systematic guard passing methodology where distance management, leg control, and pressure application converge into a unified strategic framework. The biomechanical advantage stems from the top player's ability to apply downward force through the shoulder girdle directly into the opponent's thoracic region while simultaneously controlling both lower limbs, creating a mechanical disadvantage that makes guard retention exceptionally difficult. The position's effectiveness lies not in explosive movements but in the systematic removal of the bottom player's defensive options through precise control points and weight distribution. Modern competitors who master headquarters can maintain this position indefinitely while methodically breaking down even the most sophisticated guard retention systems through patient, pressure-based passing.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Headquarters is my absolute go-to position for passing any type of guard in competition because it gives me total control with almost zero risk. When I get to headquarters, I know I'm passing—it's just a matter of which direction based on how they defend. The key is being patient and heavy, making them carry your weight until they make a mistake or get tired. I use headquarters especially against leg lockers because it keeps me safe from entries while I systematically break down their guard. From here I can go knee slice, long step, or smash depending on how they react, and I'm threatening all three at the same time so they can't defend effectively. If you're not using headquarters as your main passing position in no-gi, you're making your life way harder than it needs to be.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: While headquarters is primarily a pressure passing position, we've found ways to use it as a control point before transitioning to more dynamic attacks or even leg entanglements. The traditional approach is solid, but in 10th Planet we like to add movement and create dilemmas from this position. Instead of just grinding forward, we'll use headquarters to bait reactions—threaten the pass one way, then cut back the other direction or even transition to truck position if they turn away. You can also use it as a rest position in no-gi when you need to recover but don't want to give up your passing progress. The shoulder pressure keeps them pinned while you catch your breath and plan your next move. It's become increasingly important in modern no-gi because it's one of the few positions where you can be super safe from leg locks while still maintaining offensive pressure.
